utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, I'll address you. I'm sorry we're late starting, but the hospital appointment, as is the way of such things, was delayed. We're ready now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have one short matter to bring to the Court's attention. It is dealing with the next witness, who is apparently a Major in the Danish army, Lars Baggesen. We were presented last night with -- I'll call it an offer of proof of about 38 pages, 249 paragraphs. It looks like there are many different kinds of opinions embedded into this report about which this witness is apparently going to be requested to utter. So we would just register an objection under Rule 94 bis. I'm familiar with -- I know the Court's views that military men should be permitted to offer opinions within their area of expertise, and we accept that, but some of these opinions go into the political area, and we would object to those as being beyond the expertise of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For example, paragraph 246. The last page. We would think that that would be an objectionable opinion, as would, for example, paragraph 72 on page 11. Those are just representative of several areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, have you indicated to the Prosecution where these objections are?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have not had the opportunity to touch base with the Prosecution, but I can give you two or three more examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For example, on page 25, Your Honour, where the witness apparently is going to speak about the apparent plan that the Croats had at the highest levels, paragraph 168, 170. Those are the sorts of things that we're talking about. The witness is also apparently going to offer opinions on a matter of military subjects such as the shelling of Zenica on April the 19th, and of course, that would be a closer question that would appear to fall within the witness's expertise, provided a foundation is laid that he has artillery experience and expertise. But on the political matters, we think that's beyond the witness's competence, beyond his stated expertise and is really not particularly helpful to the Trial Chamber. On another matter, I am -- and consistent with our approach not to object generally to leading questions, I can indicate to the Trial Chamber the specific areas where we would object to leading questions by paragraph number if the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have no objections to it other than these paragraphs, paragraphs 40 to 44, 71 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us make sure we have a note of this. 40 to 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 71 and 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To which you have an objection anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And 151 and 152, 158 to 159, 162 to 164, and 168, and 170.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To which you object. 168, 170.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And 171, 192. If it would be helpful, we have an extra copy if the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, I think, regarding the principle of not being able to express political opinions, the Chamber can only but agree with you. So we will do so automatically ourselves; that is to say that an expert should come here to speak about the field of his expertise. However, as you know, you can always, by applying this method, which has, of course, produced results which-- because it has helped us to go forward more quickly. As regarding questions that should not be leading, you can say so when the time comes. The Chamber, as you know, will rule on a case-by-case basis. So there's no problem there. As for the principle, of course we are not engaging in politics here, we are in a Tribunal, so it goes without saying. As for a more general issue, you know that our rules give us a certain degree of flexibility to judge for ourselves the evidence that is produced and to assess its value. That is what I think, and I think we can proceed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to finish your matters in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, if the Court pleases. I have just a few more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You got to 192.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next one would be 202, 218, 235, and 236, and 237, 243 to 246, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Sayers. Yes, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, I would like to inform the Judges that we are sharing this opinion. We discussed that, and we have about the same feelings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Scott, we won't trouble you to argue the various points now. It can be done during the course of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Those matters being in dispute, as indicated, we have this document, and I wonder if we can take it quickly, your leading matters. If need be, you can simply refer to the matters. It may be helpful if the witness, in fact, has the document in front of him, unless there is any objection, and you can refer to the various paragraph numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour. The only question is how the record will be made. Will this statement then become part of the evidentiary record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a good point. It may be simplest if you read the paragraph referring to the paragraph, you read it out and say, "Is that right?" But I hope we can move fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll make every effort, Your Honour. I appreciate Mr. Sayers giving us these notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could then, in light of the Court's comments before the witness was brought in, if we could hand the witness, please, a copy of his outline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Hand it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. You are Major Lars Baggesen of the Danish army?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me say, procedurally, what we've agreed this morning, Major Baggesen, is that you now have in front of you an outline that's been prepared to assist in covering your testimony. As I hope is clear, it is not a script, by any means, but it will be an outline to facilitate going through your testimony. And also, in order to move as efficiently as possible, on the points that are not heavily contested, or perhaps contested at all, many of these paragraphs I will simply put to you, if you will, and you can then indicate if you agree or disagree. If you have something you feel that you must add in terms of accuracy, we will try to accommodate you. So just so you know how we're proceeding, please.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, as a preliminary matter, I understand you made a book, essentially a diary, during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have that with you today?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you testified previously in the Blaskic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your Blaskic testimony, you made reference to your diary in the course of your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to bring that to the Court's attention and make it clear that in the course of his testimony, for points of detail, Major Baggesen does have his contemporaneous -- essentially notes -- which has been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless there is any objection, the witness can refer to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence for Mr. Kordic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No objection, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, if you want to refer to your diary to check anything, you are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, is it correct, then, that you have been a career officer in the Danish army since January of 1976, and your rank at the present time is major?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you attended the Danish army combat school, where you were trained in infantry and armoured combat tactics?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I note from looking at your uniform, is it accurate to say that you are also a trained airborne officer?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you have also been trained at the Danish army special school for intelligence?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following this training, you were an intelligence officer engaged in analysing the forces of the former Soviet Bloc and Warsaw Pact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1980 to 1986, you commanded a reconnaissance platoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I understand the functions of a reconnaissance platoon, you are trained to find an enemy's front line, to fight on the enemy front line, and to do reconnaissance behind an enemy's front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, not only have you been taught yourself and carried out intelligence functions, have you also trained other Danish army intelligence officers?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of all this training and your professional military experience, is it fair to say that you are quite familiar with the infantry and armour training, tactics, and doctrine of the former Soviet Bloc and Warsaw Pact forces?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In short, Major Baggesen, is it fair to say that you are a trained, professional, and experienced military intelligence officer and military observer?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I would say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1981, you served as part of the United Nations force in Cyprus; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1986 to 1990, you were the operations officer for the Home Guard Region 5, where you were responsible for planning and carrying out military operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from 1990 to 1995, did you work for the Danish army chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1995, you were promoted to major; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are currently, again, the chief of operations for Home Guard District 53, in charge of operations and training for, is it correct, approximately 6.000 men and women?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No, I was -- before July this year, I was commanding Home Guard District 53.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: With -- at that time I had 1.600 men under my command. And now I'm chief of operations for Home Guard Region 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Then I'm in charge of the operation and training for those 6.000 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very good. And that is your current position?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to 1992, you volunteered, sir, to serve as part of the European Community Monitoring Mission, or ECMM --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you arrived in Zagreb in connection with those duties on the 30th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ECMM was the European Community Monitoring Mission first established for the former Yugoslavia in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Its general role was to observe and interact with civilian and military authorities in an assigned area for the purpose of monitoring and enforcing ceasefire and other agreements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that all of the members of the European Community Monitoring Mission were professional military men and women from different armed forces in the European Community and/or the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you dressed in conspicuous white uniforms, wore blue caps, and you were unarmed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the reason for the white uniform to help distinguish yourself from the combatants?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the overall ECMM headquarters was in Zagreb, Croatia, and under these headquarters would then be a series of what were called regional centres, and in a number of instances, under the regional centres, there would be coordination centres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us which of the offices or divisions below the Zagreb headquarters were you assigned to on your arrival in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I was assigned to the regional centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask the witness to be shown exhibits 2573 and 2575. Your Honour, there should be a packet of exhibits for each of Your Honours, and of course sets for the Defence as well. They have been -- if we've succeeded, Your Honour, the stack of exhibits should be in the order in which they will come up in Major Baggesen's testimony. So again, hopefully Exhibit 2573 should be on top. The only exception to that, Your Honour -- since I've stopped, procedurally, I'll tell the Court -- the only exception to what I just said about order is that there are some oversize exhibits, photographs and maps and things, which have been pulled -- they should be at the back, in a packet, at the bottom of your stack, which, because they don't fit into the stack, they will need to be pulled out from time to time, or at least I suggest that they will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, if you have Exhibit 2573 in front of you, is this essentially a structural chart, if you will, of the ECMM, at least as of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, concerning the RC Zenica, because there was a lot of others with, you know, centres covering the Balkans. This shows the organisation from the RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, obviously, what you're saying is if you start at the top with the Zagreb headquarters, there could be a number of regional centres on the same line with Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular one focuses on regional centre Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Down below that, and I apologise for this probably several generation copy, it's not very legible, but in the two boxes that have almost become black underneath regional centre Zenica, can you just tell the Court basically what would be the next level of organisation?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: The next level of the organisation is coordination centres, and we had a coordination in Travnik, a coordination centre in Tuzla, and a coordination centre in Mostar, and the two black boxes just underneath RC Zenica are teams who were staying in Zenica were referring directly to the regional centre. We had there, you cannot see it, but we had a team in Zepce, a team in Vares, and a team in Kakanj, and the other black box says that we have a liaison officer to UNPROFOR stationed in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. During your tour of duty, you were one of the teams operating out of the regional centre in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning, in April, the organisation was a little different. At that time we didn't have the coordination in Travnik, so we have teams going to Vitez directly from Zenica at that time. But in May, because of the increased tension in Travnik, we started up this coordination centre in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. If we can look then to the next exhibit, 2575. Can you just tell the Court briefly, we're not going to stay on these topics very long, but can you just tell the Court briefly what that document represents or is?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: This shows the standard routine team task we had. I would like to explain that. When I'm talking about a "team," each team had two monitors from different countries who had with us a driver and an interpreter. So a team was consisting of four members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And in a substantial way, was your daily task to go out with these teams into your assigned areas to essentially monitor conditions on the ground?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think the document basically speaks for itself, but a large part of your responsibility would reference, in particular, to items 2 and 3, was to regularly liase and have contact with both civil and military authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of RC Zenica itself, can you tell the Court, did that cover what was essentially known or referred to as Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include, to your knowledge, such areas as Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, you were then in Central Bosnia on your assigned duties from approximately the 2nd of April, 1993 to the 1st of July, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the -- well, I guess I can continue leading. Excuse me. Is it correct that at that time, RC Zenica was headed by a professional French diplomat named Jean-Pierre Thebault?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His deputy was a Spanish ECMM official named Juan Valentin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct, sir, that during your work in Central Bosnia, at one time or another you essentially worked in all the monitoring teams that were operating out of RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Not in all of them. I was not in the Mostar area, and I was not in the Tuzla area, but I was covering the areas as before mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you went to ECMM, were you provided some training and briefing as to what your job would be and essentially the facts on the ground, if you will, as ECMM understood them to be?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as part of that, when you were briefed -- was it explained to you that the principal Bosnian Croat political leader in Central Bosnia was Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the official ECMM assessment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also told, as part of your briefing, that the military HVO commander in Central Bosnia in the Operative Zone was Colonel Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, can you just tell the Court, this is how you were briefed at the beginning of your tour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of your tour did that assessment, in your view, based on your experience, was that accurate?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your briefing, were you told that the Bosnian Croat or HVO forces, at least at that time, were better armed and equipped than the Bosnian Muslim or ABiH forces?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, they were in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, again, was that consistent with your observations in the field that, in fact, what you saw was that the HVO tended to be better armed and equipped than the Muslims forces?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, based on your prior experience in intelligence and your training in the Danish army, did it come to your attention that the essentially Soviet Bloc or Warsaw Pact training tactics and military doctrine applied to the military forces of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So essentially in terms of command and control, essentially in areas of responsibility, in terms of lines of communication, in terms of combat doctrine, these forces tended to act consistent with the doctrine and training of the former Soviet Bloc?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in the former Yugoslavia, up until at least 1991, all young men -- and I have a note here that I forgot to ask you but I will in a moment -- had to do 12 months' national service in the JNA? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what age did this national service apply? Did that become effective at age 18, age 19?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Normally it's 18, but I don't know the correct age down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, but was it, in your knowledge and to your experience, was it the case that most of these men in Bosnia that you encountered, if you will, there were those who were over -- by the time of 1993, those who were, say, more than 20 years old, under the prior system had all had military training and experience?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, because you have been in the JNA before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they have -- again, would have been trained essentially consistent with, to your knowledge, the Soviet Bloc-type of training tactics and doctrine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your assessment, sir, that as of the spring of 1993, the HVO was more of a standard regular army at that time than, say, the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. And I based this on -- because the soldiers have been in the -- most of the soldiers have been in the JNA before. So, therefore, they were using the same equipment and tactics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of the early spring of 1993, what was your assessment of the ABiH or the Muslim armed forces?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It seems to me that the army of BH was a beaten army at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Wouldn't the soldiers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Wouldn't the soldiers of the ABiH also have been in the JNA in the same way as the soldiers of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, but they didn't have all the equipment, because when the JNA was -- what do you call it -- when it stopped to exist in 1991, the Bosnian Serb army and the HVO took over most of the equipment from the JNA, but I think that the Muslims had the same training but they didn't have the equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, is it correct then that based on your professional military experience and observations, that during your tour of duty from the 2nd of April until the 1st of July, 1993, Colonel Blaskic was the senior professional soldier in charge of the HVO armed forces in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Central Bosnia -- the HVO Central Bosnia Operative Zone included the municipalities of Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Kiseljak, Visoko, Kakanj, Fojnica, Kresevo, Gornji Vakuf, Vares, and all or part of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In reference to just on that point, could you look -- could the witness please be shown Exhibit 579?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there is no objection -- I don't think the Prosecution [sic] have any objection, I don't know why -- if the bundle of exhibits, if the same stack of exhibits could be given to the witness, that would save the usher from going back and fourth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That seems sensible. Usher, if you would give the witness all the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I also note that there are some people in the gallery and there may be other people, of course, on the monitors elsewhere, it might be -- facilitate the testimony to have some of these exhibits on the ELMO, but I'll leave that to the Court's discretion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have Exhibit 579 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In reference to what you just said, this is a -- appears to be an order by Tihomir Blaskic, dated the 30th of March, 1993, appointing various HVO military officers in the Bobovac Brigade in Vares. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first one, just for -- just to indicate on the document, the first one he appoints the chief of headquarters of the brigade, the second one he appoints the chief of intelligence affairs, and the third one he appoints the chief of what appears to be an anti-aircraft defence unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This would be consistent, would it not, sir, with your view that Colonel Blaskic's, for instance, command responsibility extended as far as the Vares area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In sum on these points, sir, is it correct that it appeared that both -- based on both your briefing and your on-the-ground experience, that the HVO appeared to be a well-organised army and that Colonel Blaskic was commanding a well-organised army?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, it seems like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your experience, was it generally the case that Colonel Blaskic -- then Colonel Blaskic's orders were usually obeyed by his subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a particular example, is it correct, sir, that in the course of your duties with the ECMM, if you were out in the field and going through an HVO checkpoint, was it generally the case that if you had a written order signed by Colonel Blaskic that you would have no trouble getting through a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Not if you have a written order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me direct your attention to -- on the 14th of May of 1993, in the course of your duties, you had a meeting with some representatives of the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Travnik. In the course of that meeting, sir, is it correct that one of the HVO representatives provided you with a listing of the various brigades -- well, the command structure, if you will, and the brigades in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can look, please, at Exhibit 863. This is obviously an English version, but do you know this to be an English translation of the document that you were provided by the HVO officer on the 14th of --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a list that my interpreter translated to me and handed over to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just to orient, to give everyone some orientation to the document, at the top of the page -- and I apologise that the left side is a bit off the paper, but it seems to have gotten to the point where whatever original better copy that may have existed, it could not be, at least, readily located -- the leader of the HVO at the -- what would be the Operative Zone, which I think is the missing letter there at the left at the top would be OZMB, Operative Zone middle Bosnia, that would be Colonel Blaskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then were you also given his telephone number the location of his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, for instance, in his case we know his headquarters was located in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your on-the-ground experience, sir, did that turn out to be, in fact, accurate?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That is accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just -- as a couple of additional examples, if we go down to about the fifth box on the left column, the indication was that in terms of the Vitez Brigade, that Mr. Mario Cerkez was the commander of that brigade. His telephone number was given to you and it was indicated that his headquarters were in the Vitez cinema. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just at one more, the Busovaca Brigade, the one right below that, would be indicated to be -- the commanding officer being Dusko Grubesic, and his headquarters being in what was called the Sumarija or the Forester's Cabin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, all of these commanders of brigades, below the first line, which covers Colonel Blaskic, all these other units were essentially subordinate to his command?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that included the brigades and HVO military in Kiseljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just as an example, about the middle of the page, the Ban Jelacic Brigade, that was the Kiseljak HVO essentially; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your experience sir, and your briefings, can you tell the Court, who was the most powerful HVO political leader -- at least in your view -- in Central Bosnia during your time?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: As we were told in the beginning, and as I later on explained, it was Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, this was more than your personal view, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the official ECMM assessment?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you share with the Court any observations you have or can make about the working relationship between Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic? What did you see about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: An objection to that question in the absence of an appropriate foundation, Your Honour, i.e., that the witness actually did see Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic operating together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll find that out when he answers the question. Yes, Major.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Several times we saw Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- all right. Let's go on, and we'll come back, perhaps, to your -- did you see Mr. Kordic in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Sometimes he was wearing military uniforms, sometimes he was wearing civilian dress, and sometimes a mix of the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you ever see Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic together at the HVO headquarters in Vitez, for instance?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Central Bosnia, did you have occasion to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, excuse me for interrupting you for a moment. The witness tells us that he saw Mr. Dario Kordic in a uniform. What type of uniform? Could he remember what kind of uniform he wore and whether there were any insignia on that uniform?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: When Mr. Kordic was in uniform, he was wearing the same uniforms as other soldiers. I cannot remember to have seen any insignia on -- I cannot remember if he had any rank showing on his uniform or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following up on your earlier question, then, is it correct, sir, that on a number of occasions during your tour of duty, that you saw Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic together?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your time on the ground there, did you have any knowledge of how Mr. Kordic, for instance, was portrayed by the Bosnian Croat local media? How did they present Mr. Kordic, if you will?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: They presented Mr. Kordic as the political leader in the region, and he often had a comment in the local news, in the local papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet a man in the course of your duties named -- a Bosnian Croat leader named Pero Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Skopljak indicate to you or make a statement to you about Mr. Kordic's role in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I was working together -- in the end of my period in Bosnia, I was working together with Mr. Skopljak, and Mr. Skopljak told me that Mr. Kordic was the political leader in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on all these observations and your experience, can you relate, then, the -- is it correct to say Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic together, then, were the two senior HVO leaders in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your training in the Danish army, sir, did you have a -- what might be referred to as a specialist badge in communications?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's, in fact, one of the insignias on, I think, the right side of your chest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, is it correct that the HVO was in charge of the PTT or telephone facilities and lines in the areas of Vitez, Travnik, and Kiseljak? And I might add, is it correct, Busovaca as well?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your experience, could you see and observe that the HVO components or organisations in Central Bosnia were able to communicate with each other through a telephone network and through a fax network?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that on a number of occasions, Major Baggesen, you were able to observe HVO communication capabilities, from seeing antennas, to seeing radio equipment and operators, to seeing such things as fax machines?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also see that the HVO was able to communicate through a field radio communication network?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, on a number of occasions, were you actually able to see or observe these networks in operations, both at the main HVO headquarters in Vitez and at various other HVO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. Normally they didn't want us to see that they had the radio equipment, but on some occasions we were able to see them anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that normally they did not want you to see the communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It's normal for an army to try to hide what they have of communications equipment, not to show the other part that they are able to have more or less sophisticated radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in fact, you understood that in addition to all the communication capabilities that you've described in the last couple of minutes, that it was to your knowledge that the HVO had other or additional more sophisticated communication capabilities?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time during your tour in Central Bosnia that the telephone company in Zenica wanted to reconnect the telephone lines between Zenica and Sarajevo, and it came to your attention or to ECMM's attention that the telephone line had apparently been cut somewhere in the vicinity of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you went to the PTT office in Kiseljak, which was under HVO control; you subsequently found the actual PTT engineer in Kresevo, and he told you that the phone lines at the PTT building in Kiseljak had been damaged by shelling and not repaired?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also accurate to say that this PTT engineer told you that it would be easy enough to repair the telephone line, and all that was needed was a written order from either Colonel Blaskic or Vinko Lucic, the commander of the HVO military police in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have occasion then to meet with the head of the PTT office in Kiseljak, who essentially told you the same story, that the telephone line had been cut by shelling?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he express to you that he really, himself, could not see any reason to fix the line, because in his view it was not necessary for Zenica to have any contact with Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it accurate to say, sir, that at that time, the majority ethnic community in Zenica was Muslim, and the majority ethnic community under siege in Sarajevo was also Muslim?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion, sir, then to investigate the alleged shelling at the PTT building in Kiseljak and determine whether in fact you thought shelling had broken or damaged the telephone line?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. We went to see the PT building and the equipment, and we were able to see there was one minor -- maybe two minor impacts on the building, but it was not enough to make any damages on the equipment. So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: We were sure that the telephone lines had been just cut for the purpose not to let the Muslims have contact between Zenica and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at Exhibit 858,3. Is that a copy, sir, of your daily ECMM report for 1 May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2 -- well, actually both paragraphs 1 and 2, I suppose, are in reference to your work, if you will, in connection with the telephone lines and the particular connection in Kiseljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a professional military officer and as a specialist in communications, sir, can you tell us, was it in your experience and observation that the Bosnian Croats and the HVO forces had an effective communications system in place in 1993 and was generally able to communicate with its various components and forces when it wanted to?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. And they were able to control the PT lines as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your understanding, by the way, that the ECMM telephone calls, your own telephone calls, were being monitored by HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Not -- not in Zenica, but we had another headquarters at a house in Vitez, close to the British Battalion, and at that time we were using the PTT in Vitez. Sometimes we were able to use the PT lines, and other times we were not able to use it, and we were told by a Croat interpreter that the reason for us not to able to -- or the reason that sometimes the PT line had been cut was because there was no one at the PTT building in Vitez that was able to speak English, and that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the ability --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: But we only have his word on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: But it's a normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The issue of the ability to speak English was to understand the -- their ability to understand the conversations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, to listen to our conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, was it the ECMM official policy that any sensitive or classified information should not be discussed on the PTT lines?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's a normal security procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your work in Central Bosnia, are there many times -- and we're going to hear about it in the course of your testimony -- when you would be out in the field, going to HVO facilities, going to HVO checkpoints, can you tell the Court whether -- is it true that it was your experience that in a number of instances, it was clear that your whereabouts or your coming had been communicated ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, because very often, when we were going to visit a brigade commander or another facility, it seemed that they were prepared; that they knew that we were coming. And the only way they could know was if someone had told them that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to spend a few minutes talking about something called the Busovaca Joint Commission. When you arrived in Zenica in early April of 1993, did you become a member of what was called the Busovaca Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you briefed, in fact, about that commission at that time by another Danish ECMM monitor named Erik Friis-Pedersen?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. He was chairing the Busovaca Joint Commission at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it accurate to say, sir, that the Busovaca Joint Commission was a commission that had been formed by the ECMM, UNPROFOR, the HVO, and the ABiH in early 1993 to try to address and solve problems and conflicts between the Croat and Muslim forces in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, had that commission, to your knowledge, essentially come out of the armed conflict that had broken out about the end of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was the purpose of the Busovaca Joint Commission, again, to solve problems, build trust among the various parties, and maintain or foster peace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could look, then, at Exhibit 512. Is this, just briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, when you come to a convenient break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We can finish this one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a copy of essentially what you understood to be a founding document, or charter, if you will, for the Busovaca Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I assure both you and the Court we're not going to go through the document in any great detail. Looking at the second page, one of the persons who played a role at the time in forming the commission was Colonel Stewart; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the last page -- and we'll come back to this after the break, I believe, but as long as we have the document in front of us now, is it correct that there was an overall structure, and at essentially every level, there would be an ECMM representative; sometimes, in that particular area, a BritBat representative; and then you would have at least one representative from the HVO side and one representative from the ABiH side? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you get down to the level of Team -- toward the bottom of the page, Team 1 and Team 2, what were those teams -- I'll just pick Team 1 for an example. What would Team 1 do on a daily -- what did they do?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Normally, when we had a meeting in the commission, we started in the house in Vitez at 7.00 in the morning, and we had a discussion around the table, and the HVO were telling what had been happening, incidents in the last 24 hours, and then the BiH told what they had seen of incidents the last 24 hours. And after that, we formed teams; two, maybe three teams, and then we went to a spot to do fact-finding. Because there were a lot of rumours down there, and sometimes we heard -- maybe the HVO told us that there had been a massacre on a village, and then we went to the village to see if it was correct or if it just was a rumour. And sometimes it was correct, and other times it was a rumour, but it was important for us to go to the spot to see what had been happening, doing some fact-finding. And if it only was a rumour, to communicate that to the local public relations, to tell them that everything is calm and there's nothing to be afraid of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can stop there, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll take a short break now. Ten minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, Baggesen, I've been reminded by the interpreters to speak more slowly, and between the two of us, and since I'm doing the talking, I'm afraid it's mostly my fault, but between the answer and question, if we can both break, especially for the interpreters, it would be easier for them.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The Busovaca Joint Commission then, is it correct -- just to bring everyone to the same point, I'm looking now at paragraph 65 of the outline -- is it correct that the usual leader of the HVO delegation was Franjo Nakic, who was the HVO deputy commander to Colonel Blaskic of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The usual leader of the ABiH delegation was Dzemal Merdan, who was the deputy commander of the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, as I understand it, the history of the commission was that it was originally located in Busovaca and then later moved to Vitez, I think primarily to be closer to BritBat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned before the break that you would have these daily early-morning meetings. One side or the other or both may make various complaints or protests about alleged events. They would essentially be allowed to say their piece, and then teams would be formed to investigate the allegations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Typically what would happen is these teams, consisting of the ECMM monitors, Dzemal Merdan for the ABiH, Franjo Nakic for the HVO, along with the interpreters, would then go to the places or make further inquiry as to the allegations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, sir, that Mr. Merdan had more authority to act and deal with these matters as they arose, without having to get additional direction or authorisation from his superior authorities?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other side of the coin, did it appear to you that Franjo Nakic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. This is an area, which as I understand it, is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't understand that 69 was, Your Honour, but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, 69, let's take it from here as being in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you relate to the Court, in reference to the participation of the representatives of the ABiH side and the HVO side, when the team would want to go to, say, an HVO facility or location, a location controlled by HVO, what would Mr. Nakic have to do?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Very often we will have to pass the HVO headquarters at Hotel Vitez to get a written order from Colonel Blaskic that allowed us to go to that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That was in most of the times. On the opposite side, if we were going to BiH occupied area, there was normally no problems to go there. Then it was enough that Mr. Merdan was with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you become familiar, in the course of your time in Central Bosnia, with something called the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, did --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm jumping, for the moment, Your Honour, to paragraph 73.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you'd been to Central Bosnia for a couple of weeks or so, were you, in fact, briefed, not only you, but the RC Zenica ECMM staff, on the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were briefed -- excuse me. You were briefed on that by Ambassador Thebault?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, and I'm sure it could be much more -- we could go into this in much more detail, but the basic notion of the Vance-Owen Plan was that essentially the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be divided up into a series of provinces or cantons and essentially apportioned out, if you will, to be governed by the majority ethnic group in that particular province or canton; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, it was proposed that there would be approximately some ten provinces --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm looking now, Your Honour, at paragraph 74. I'm jumping around here a bit, Your Honour, to avoid leading, but we'll get to the same place, if you'll allow me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were ten proposed provinces or cantons?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can look at Exhibit 2574. 2574. It's a map or drawing. Major Baggesen, is Exhibit 2574 a copy of a map of Bosnia that you actually took from -- copied from a Bosnian Croat newspaper during your time in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can't remember if it was from a Bosnian Croat. I think it was maybe from a BH, maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. From a local newspaper?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, from a local newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the document there are a number of bold, black lines, if you will. Are those the lines between the proposed provinces?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. The border lines between the different provinces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on of the left side of the document there are numbered boxes and names. Were those the provinces by number and also were these the proposed, at least at some point the proposed names for each of the provinces?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your attention, for instance -- we'll start at the bottom of the list -- the proposed province number 10 would be called Travnicka?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or Travnicka. Sorry. On the map there, and again my an apologies for the quality, but about the middle of Bosnia, in the circle a number 10; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was going to be the Travnicka canton or province 10; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then looking to the number 8, there was going to be a province called -- referred to as Mostarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that among the various cantons, that provinces 8 and 10 were going to be proposed, in the course of discussions about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, as Croat provinces?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just -- we're not going to talk about this in terms of our particular area, but just so the record is clear, there was a third Bosnian Croat province, number 3, which is up in the top of the country, Your Honours, marked number 3, and I just point that out for clarification's sake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are these your notes by the box, if you will, by the list, in terms of the ethnic make-up of the provinces?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No. The original was in black and white, and I asked my interpreter just to colour it and to mention what was the sort of populations in the different provinces. As you can see, province 10, 8, and 3, they are quite mixed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: "Quite mixed" means that the majority in those provinces are Croats, and then there's a majority [sic] Of Muslims and maybe Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we come back to some other points, is it correct that province 10 would include the municipalities -- in reference to paragraph 77, Your Honours -- Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Gornji Vakuf, Donji Vakuf, Jajce, Fojnica, Bogojna, Kupres, Duvno, and Livno?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at the map, is it correct to say that both cantons of province 10 and 8 would then border on the Republic of Croatia to the south and west? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go to province 9. If we look on the chart, that is to be described, at least here, known as Zenicka, and that was indicated here as being a Muslim mixed province; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were briefed on the Vance-Owen Plan and saw this and maps like it, did it become a concern not only held by you but held by others at the ECMM, that the Vance-Owen Plan might, in fact, reinforce or promote ethnic division in Bosnia as opposed to accomplish peace?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: The official was that the Vance-Owen Plan was a good plan, but there were a lot of individuals that didn't like this plan because we were afraid that this plan would increase the problems in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, by the end of your tour at the end of June or early July of 1993, looking back, would it be your assessment that, in fact, at least as interpreted or applied by one or more of the parties, that, in fact, the Vance-Owen Plan did become a part of the increased reason for the increased tensions and conflict in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, I think that calls for or tiptoes into the area of political opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's only a tiptoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I won't go further, Your Honour, except to respond that again, I think this was in the course of the ECMM's role and his responsibilities of monitoring and liasing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the fairest way dealing with the controversial evidence is for the witness to be asked what happened and then to tell us, if he would, quite factually, without involving opinions, because of course much of the controversial matter is what we're going to have to decide, on all the evidence, as to what actually were the motives of those involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at -- looking again, and sticking to the facts, if we look at the Exhibit 2574 --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- is it correct to say that when one looks at the borders between proposed province 10 and proposed province 9, at least the commonly-shared borders, one can see, in fact, the territory that's largely described in the facts of this case? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the three months in Bosnia, did you see population shifts among the ethnic groups across that line, if you will? And by that I mean the line between central -- excuse me; the line between province 9 and province 10.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell the Court in your own words what you saw.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: What we saw when we were trying to implement this plan was that there was a lot of ethnic cleansing in that area. It seemed to us that the HVO wanted to get rid of all the Muslims in province number 10, and they wanted to have as many as possible Croats taken out of Zenica -- that's belonging to province number 9 -- and move them to province number 10. And as I earlier, in my earlier statement and testimony, told you, the Court, it was not only an opinion made by ECMM; it was the opinion made by UNPROFOR as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that regard, please, can I show you and direct the courtroom's attention to Exhibit 390,2. I want to direct your attention, please, to paragraph 2 on the first page. And again, to assist the interpreters as much as possible, would you just read paragraph 2 as clearly and slowly, within reason, as you can?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: "The tensions seem to be most severe in areas where there is no clear majority of either ethnic group in a particular opstina. Jablanica, (majority Muslim) from experiencing the effects of ethnic turmoil. Over the past week, the political and military leaders of the Croatian Community of HERCEG-BOSNA have begun to implement their 'understanding' of the proposed settlement for the conflict in BH. This premature and imperfect grab for control of provinces 3, 8, and 10 has resulted in extremely high tensions in these and enjoining areas,"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slow down, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: "and heavy fighting between Muslim and Croat units in and around GORNJI VAKUF."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is, please, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a report of UNPROFOR command in Kiseljak, actually signed by -- you'll notice in the upper box on the page, on the right, signed by Brigadier Cordy-Simpson, dated the 24th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just register a brief objection to this, Your Honour. This document was obviously -- and it speaks for itself, but it was obviously drafted before the witness's arrival in Central Bosnia, and I wonder if he has ever seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, no doubt that's a point you can make. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question following on that, Major Baggesen, was, in your experience in Central Bosnia, did this assessment essentially -- which may have started, in fact, before you arrived in Central Bosnia -- continue to be the assessment of many, not only among ECMM, but also at UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention next to Exhibit 612. Perhaps it's worth spending one moment on this document, because the Court will probably see many of these documents in the course of the remainder of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So if I explain this one, Your Honour, in a little bit of detail, the rest will be, hopefully, clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have Exhibit 612 in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This appears to be a report, an ECMM report. And at this particular level, looking at the cover sheet, essentially a fax cover page, can you tell the Court, and for the record, from where is this document coming or report coming, and to whom is it being made?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: This is a report made by our ECMM headquarters in Zagreb. Every day ECMM headquarters in Zagreb made this, daily monitor activity, based on all the reports they had from all the RCs. Therefore you would be able to see reports from RC Zagreb, from RC Knin, RC Zenica, RC Szeged in Hungary, and RC Belgrade, RC Skopje, and RC Tirana. So this is a combined report of all the reports, all the headquarters in Zagreb had from the RCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be a fair description of the reporting procedure that you, as an individual monitor, would make a daily report, at least one of which we've already seen, the monitor's reports at the local level would generate a local, for instance, RC Zenica report, the various regional centres would essentially collate their report, and then they would be communicated at increasing compilations of the levels up to a composite report to the senior headquarters or the senior diplomatic community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this particular document, then, would you look -- can I direct your attention to page 2. "Page 2 of 4" is the actual way it's described at the bottom of the page, paragraph 12. In reference to that paragraph 12, could you please read that statement into the record.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It just says: "On 4th April, Mate Boban, leader of the Bosnian Croats, urged the Bosnian Herzegovina President Izetbegovic to apply without delay the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. According to Mr. Boban, this would mean that the Muslim army retire from the provinces designated to become Croat or accept to be under the Bosnian Croat army command."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the reference -- when there's the reference to the three provinces, to your knowledge, sir, that would be provinces 3, 8, and 10; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Consistent with those two documents and the discussion -- or excuse me, your testimony over the last few minutes, as the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan came to be more discussed and more subject of your daily, essentially, meetings, did you find that the behaviour of the Bosnian Croat side changed or took on a different direction with the implementation or proposed implementation of that plan?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It seemed to us that the Bosnian Croats maybe had another opinion on how this plan should be carried out. It was understood in the peace plan that the population in the provinces should be a mixed population with the Croats and Muslims. But as we see it, the Croat -- Bosnian Croat understanding was that it should be an ethnically clean province in those three provinces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that they would become something, if not pure, but close to pure Croat provinces?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, moving ahead, is it correct, sir, that on about the 12th of April of 1993, you and other ECMM members were invited by Colonel Blaskic to an Easter celebration at the HVO headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that both Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic were at the celebration?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, they were both there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how Mr. Kordic introduced himself?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: He introduced himself as president -- or vice-president of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he identify himself as an official or leader with any other entity or organisation?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Well, he identified himself as he was a political leader in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall, from your discussions or the times that you heard Mr. Kordic speak, when he talked about the country as part of the former Yugoslavia known as Bosnia-Herzegovina, did he talk about it in terms of saying "Bosnia-Herzegovina," or did he speak of it consistently in terms of "Herceg-Bosna"?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Normally, when Mr. Kordic was discussing that, he was using "Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, around the time of the Easter celebration, had there been a particular event close by in Travnik that had caused some turmoil, to begin?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, actually because during this Easter celebration, Mr. Thebault, who was head of RC Zenica, he was a little delayed for the celebration because he went to Travnik, because there had been some problems in Travnik concerning some flag raising. The Croat population in Travnik had begun to fly the Croatian flag and not the official flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That creates problems in the area, and when Ambassador Thebault went to Travnik, he was stopped in a checkpoint and he was forced back. The HVO checkpoint pointed their weapons against him and forced him out. So he was not able to go to Travnik. So he was a little delayed for this celebration, and he was very upset when he arrived to the celebration. And actually, because we wanted to go to Travnik to monitor the situation in the area, because we think that it would be a major problem if the Croats were going to use the Croatian flag in this population, that was at that time, I think that the Croats were a minority in Travnik, and of course the Muslim or the Bosniaks in that area wanted that official flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be used up there. So therefore, together with another monitor, after the celebration, we went to Travnik. We were not allowed to go there, because Mr. Thebault told us it was too dangerous to go up there, but we felt it was necessary to go up there. So we went to monitor the situation in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before we go to talk about your trip to Travnik, is it fair to say, then, Major Baggesen, that the flying of the Croatian flag was known to be provocative to the Muslim community at this time?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the Easter celebration, did both Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic make speeches?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm directing your attention to Exhibit 670, 6-7-0. Did it come to your attention, around this time, that Mr. Kordic did encourage or, in fact, was encouraging the flying or displaying of the Croatian flag?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: We knew that he had his fingerprint on it, if you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I object to that opinion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why? If it is something the witness knows about, he can tell us. He's put it in graphic terms. Perhaps, Major, you could tell us why the accuse Mr. Kordic had his fingerprint on it?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Because we knew from a statement in some of the local media that he asked them. Kordic and other Croat political leaders asked the population to raise the Croatian flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
